title: From Containers to Orchestration
tagline: Why containers exist, what Kubernetes adds, and the pieces of a cluster
overview: This chapter starts with the problem containers solve, compares them with virtual machines, and shows how an image is built and run. It then explains what Kubernetes does on top of containers, when it is the wrong tool, how it differs from Docker Swarm, and the main parts of a cluster.

topics.question: What is a container, and what problem does it solve?
topics.say_first: A container is a packaged, isolated process that carries its code, runtime and libraries with it, so it behaves the same on a laptop, in test and in production.
explain: Think of a shipping container. The crane does not care whether it holds shoes or engines, because the box is a standard size and sealed. A software container does the same for an application: whatever is inside, every machine knows how to run the box.

The classic pain is 'it works on my machine'. The app depended on a library version or setting that only existed on the developer's laptop. Packing the app together with those dependencies removes the difference between environments.
The packaged form is called an image. A container is a running instance of that image, and it normally runs one main process (the entrypoint) isolated from the host and from other containers.
key_points: Image = the package; container = a running copy of it.
Contains code, runtime, system libraries and settings, not a whole operating system.
Same image runs identically from development to production.
Usually one main process per container.
Isolation keeps one container from interfering with its neighbours.

pitfalls: Calling a container 'a small VM'. It shares the host kernel and is just an isolated process.

topics.question: How are container images built, and why are they made of layers?
topics.say_first: Each Dockerfile instruction adds a read-only layer, so images are built and shipped incrementally and unchanged layers are reused from cache.
explain: A Dockerfile is a recipe. Every step (choose a base, copy files, install packages) produces a new layer stacked on the previous one, like transparent sheets laid over each other.
If you change only your application code, only the top layers are rebuilt and re-uploaded. The base layers are already cached locally and in the registry, so builds and pulls are fast.
When a container starts, a thin writable layer is placed on top of the read-only image layers. Writes go there (copy-on-write) and disappear when the container is removed.
key_points: One layer per instruction; layers are immutable and shareable.
Order instructions from least to most frequently changed to maximise cache hits.
Many containers can share the same image layers on one host.
The writable container layer is temporary storage.

topics.question: What is the difference between containers and virtual machines?
topics.say_first: A VM virtualises hardware and runs a full guest OS; a container virtualises the operating system and shares the host kernel, so it is far lighter and starts in seconds.
explain: A VM is a pretend computer. A hypervisor carves one physical server into several virtual ones, and each gets its own complete operating system, which is heavy.

A container is more like a separate apartment in one building. Everyone shares the same plumbing (the host kernel) but has their own locked door and rooms (isolated processes, filesystem and network).
That sharing is why containers are small, boot quickly and pack densely. It is also why isolation is weaker than with VMs: a kernel flaw affects every container on the host.
key_points: VM: hypervisor plus a guest kernel per VM; GBs and slow boot.
Container: shared host kernel; MBs and near-instant start.
Containers need the same kernel type as the host (Linux containers need a Linux kernel).
VMs give stronger isolation and can run different operating systems side by side.

topics.question: Which Linux kernel features make containers possible?
topics.say_first: Namespaces for isolation, cgroups for resource limits, and a union (overlay) filesystem for layered, copy-on-write images.
explain: A container is not a kernel object. It is a normal Linux process that the kernel has been told to restrict using three tools.
Namespaces control what the process can see: its own process IDs, network stack, mount points, hostname, IPC and user IDs. It feels like having its own machine.
Control groups (cgroups) control what it can use: CPU, memory, I/O. This is what Kubernetes limits translate into. Overlay filesystems stitch image layers into a single view with a writable top.
key_points: Namespaces: pid, net, mnt, ipc, uts, user.
cgroups: cap and account CPU, memory and I/O.
overlayfs: stacks read-only layers with a writable layer using copy-on-write.
Exceeding a memory cgroup limit gets the process OOM-killed.

topics.question: How do you containerize an application?
topics.say_first: Write a Dockerfile, build it into an image, then run containers from that image; the same image is promoted unchanged through every environment.
explain: Step one is the Dockerfile: the commands you would have typed by hand to prepare the app (pick a base, copy code, install dependencies, set the start command) written down once.
Step two is the build, producing an image. Step three is running a container from it. To share it across machines you push the image to a registry and pull it elsewhere.
The key idea for interviews is that you build once and run anywhere; you do not rebuild per environment, you change configuration instead.
key_points: Dockerfile, build, run is the core loop.
Registries (Docker Hub, ECR, GCR) distribute images.
Use small base images and a non-root user.
Keep configuration out of the image; inject it at runtime.

topics.question: When would you choose containers, and when would you still choose VMs?
topics.say_first: Choose containers for fast, consistent, scalable microservice deployments; choose VMs when you need full OS isolation, a different OS, or an app that expects a whole machine.
explain: Containers win on consistency, density, speed and easy scaling. Because they are small, you can start dozens in the time a VM boots.
VMs still make sense when workloads need a different kernel or OS, strict tenant separation, or legacy software that assumes it owns the whole server.
In practice the two combine: containers usually run on top of VMs, which are the nodes of a cloud Kubernetes cluster.
key_points: Containers: consistency, efficiency, isolation per service, quick scale and deploy.
VMs: different OS types, complete isolation, whole-machine workloads.
Not either/or; most clusters run containers on VM nodes.

topics.question: What is Kubernetes and why do we need it?
topics.say_first: Kubernetes is an open source orchestrator that deploys, scales, heals and updates containerized applications across a group of machines, driven by a declared desired state.
explain: Running one container is easy. Running hundreds across many servers, keeping them healthy, updating them without downtime and scaling with traffic is not. Kubernetes is the conductor that keeps all those players in time.
You do not tell it every step. You describe what you want (for example, three copies of this app, version 2) and it keeps working until reality matches that description.
It handles placement, restarts, rollouts and rollbacks, service discovery, load distribution, autoscaling and attaching storage.
key_points: Often shortened to k8s.
Deploys the same app consistently across many locations or nodes.
Rolls out updates to many containers gradually and can roll back.
Scales up under load and down when quiet.
Works from desired state rather than step-by-step scripts.

topics.question: What are the key features of Kubernetes?
topics.say_first: Self-healing, load balancing, automated rollouts and rollbacks, autoscaling, a declarative model, persistent storage and extensibility through operators.
explain: Self-healing: failed containers are restarted and Pods are replaced, with no human paged for routine failures.
Rollouts and rollbacks: updates go in phases, and if a new version misbehaves you can return to the last good one. You can also pause and resume a rollout.

Autoscaling and load balancing spread traffic over healthy Pods and add or remove capacity. Storage can be attached dynamically so data outlives a container, and operators extend the API with application-specific automation.
key_points: Declarative desired state continuously enforced.
Rolling updates, pause, resume and rollback.
Horizontal scaling by metrics such as CPU.
Operators are controllers that encode operational knowledge for an app.
Persistent volumes keep data beyond a container's life.

topics.question: How does Kubernetes self-heal? Walk through what happens when a Pod crashes.
topics.say_first: A controller continuously compares desired state with actual state; when a Pod disappears it creates a replacement through the API server, the scheduler places it and a kubelet starts it.
explain: Picture a thermostat. You set 21 degrees; it measures the room and switches heating on or off until they match. Kubernetes controllers do the same with Pods. This control loop is called reconciliation.
Say a Deployment wants three replicas and one Pod dies. The kubelet reports the failure to the API server. The controller manager sees two out of three and asks the API server to create a new Pod.
The new Pod has no node yet, so the scheduler picks one and records it. The kubelet on that node notices a Pod assigned to it and asks the runtime to start it. Nobody typed a command.
key_points: Everything flows through the API server; components watch it, they do not call each other directly.
Desired state is stored in etcd; actual state is reported by kubelets.
The loop never stops, so it also fixes drift, not only crashes.
Node failure triggers the same loop, with Pods rescheduled elsewhere.

topics.question: When should you not use Kubernetes?
topics.say_first: When the cost and complexity outweigh the benefit: small teams, simple stable apps, tight budgets, or workloads that do not need scaling or high availability.
explain: Kubernetes brings many moving parts and a real learning curve. If you run three containers for a small team, the platform can cost more effort than the application.
A stable monolith that rarely changes gains little from rolling updates and autoscaling, and moving it may be hard. Leaving it where it is can be the right engineering call.
Managed offerings such as EKS, GKE or AKS take the control plane off your hands, which narrows the gap. You still own application, networking and security decisions.
key_points: Steep learning curve and operational overhead.
Overkill for small teams or few services with no scaling needs.
Legacy monoliths may be hard to migrate and gain little.
Managed control planes reduce, but do not remove, the burden.

topics.question: How does Kubernetes differ from Docker Swarm?
topics.say_first: Swarm is simpler and quicker to set up, built into Docker; Kubernetes is more complex but far more featureful, runtime-agnostic and richer in scaling, rollback and networking.
explain: Swarm comes with Docker and starts with a couple of commands. That simplicity is its main selling point, along with fast scaling of services.
Kubernetes needs extra pieces such as a network plugin and an ingress controller, but gives you autoscaling, automatic rollbacks, a flat Pod network, and a large ecosystem.

Runtime flexibility is another difference: Swarm requires Docker Engine on its nodes, while Kubernetes talks to any runtime that implements the Container Runtime Interface, such as containerd or CRI-O.
key_points: Swarm: easy setup, Docker-only, fewer features.
Kubernetes: steeper setup, pluggable runtime, large ecosystem.
Kubernetes has a distributed, highly available control plane option.
Swarm lacks automatic rollback on failed updates.

topics.question: What are the main components of a Kubernetes cluster?
topics.say_first: A cluster has a control plane that decides (API server, scheduler, controller manager, etcd) and worker nodes that run workloads (kubelet, kube-proxy, container runtime).
explain: Imagine a restaurant. The control plane is the front-of-house manager and kitchen board: it takes orders, decides who cooks what and remembers everything. Worker nodes are the cooking stations that actually prepare the dishes.

The API server is the single front door that validates and handles all requests. etcd stores the cluster data. The scheduler assigns new Pods to nodes. The controller manager runs the loops that keep reality matching your declarations.
On each worker the kubelet is the local agent managing Pods, kube-proxy programs network rules so Services work, and a container runtime such as containerd runs the containers.
key_points: Control plane = brain; worker nodes = muscle.
Only the API server talks to etcd.
Kubelet manages Pods on its node and reports status.
Kube-proxy implements Service networking on the node.
A cloud controller manager links the cluster to cloud APIs for load balancers and volumes.

topics.question: Why did Kubernetes move away from Docker Engine, and what runs containers now?
topics.say_first: The kubelet speaks the Container Runtime Interface; Docker Engine did not implement it natively and needed a shim, so Kubernetes standardised on CRI runtimes such as containerd and CRI-O.
explain: Kubernetes wanted to be runtime-neutral, so it defined a standard API, the CRI, that the kubelet uses to ask for pods and containers to be created.
Docker Engine predates it and needed an adapter called dockershim inside the kubelet. Maintaining that adapter was costly, and Docker adds extra layers Kubernetes does not need.

containerd, which Docker itself uses internally, and CRI-O implement CRI directly and follow the OCI standards for images and runtimes. Images built with Docker still run fine, because the image format is standard.
key_points: CRI is the contract between kubelet and runtime.
dockershim was removed from Kubernetes in version 1.24.
containerd and CRI-O are the common choices.
Docker-built images keep working since they follow OCI.

topics.question: What is the smallest valid Kubernetes cluster, and what does managed Kubernetes take off your plate?
topics.say_first: A cluster needs at least a control plane; with zero workers it runs, but cannot host ordinary workloads. Managed services run and patch the control plane for you.
explain: The control plane alone is a working cluster in the sense that the API answers. But Pods need a node to run on, so applications stay Pending until a worker joins. Single-node dev clusters get around this by letting the control plane node also run workloads.

With managed Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS) the provider operates the API server, etcd and other control plane parts, handles upgrades and availability, and integrates with cloud load balancers and storage.
You still choose node sizes, upgrade timing for workers, networking, access control and what runs on the cluster.
key_points: Control plane required; workers needed to run apps.
Pods without a node stay Pending.
Managed offerings remove control plane operations only.
Dev tools like kind or minikube bundle everything in one node.
